1. The frames show a grid of tiles. Each column is a start month, running from January 1991 to July 2016. Each tile is marked "lit" if buying was ahead of renting after ten years, or "dark" if renting was ahead. The source labels are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The animation is tagged "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. The grid fills in from left to right across the frames. In frame 1, many early columns are lit, a band in the middle is dark, and the right side is still unlit. A caption then appears: "lit again: every start 2009 to mid-2016". In the later frames the right side lights up. By frame 6 almost every column is lit except one dark band in the middle. A small block icon sits at the right edge and doesn't seem to change.

3. In the US data, buying beat renting after ten years for most start dates. The exception is a band of start dates in the middle of the range. Those starts are probably the mid-2000s, when buyers bought near the housing peak and then faced the crash. Buyers who started from 2009 to mid-2016 came out ahead every time. The result depends on when you buy, and it is a record of the past.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might take away that buying has usually paid off over a ten-year horizon in the US. They might also take away that buying at a market peak can make renting come out ahead. For you, the picture suggests that how long you stay and when you buy matter a lot.

5. The advice in 4 is my own reading. The on-screen text only describes the data ("buyer ahead", "renter ahead", "history, not a forecast"). It doesn't tell anyone to buy or rent. The "history, not a forecast" label warns against treating the pattern as a prediction.
